bridges.note: Both provisions establish general equality before the law, prohibit discrimination on similar grounds, and require state measures for gender equality, though the Swiss text adds specific rules on equal pay and disability.
Both provisions protect belief and conscience, but the German text also expressly includes an anti-conscription clause that the Swiss article does not.
Both provisions regulate when and how a person may be deprived of liberty, including prompt judicial review, but the German text adds specific rules on police custody and anti-mistreatment language.
Both provisions protect human dignity as a constitutional principle; A adds broader binding effect and a reference to human rights, while B states the protection more briefly.
Both provisions state that judges are independent in their adjudicative role and bound only by the law, though the German text also adds detailed tenure and removal protections.
Both provisions criminalize the intentional disclosure of secret information obtained through a professional or official role, even after the person has left that role.
Both provisions guarantee the right to submit petitions/complaints to public authorities, though the Swiss text adds an explicit prohibition on disadvantages and a duty for authorities to take note.
Both provisions protect the freedom to choose and practice a profession, but the German rule also expressly covers workplace and training choice and includes detailed limits on compulsory work.

Both provisions let an insolvency representative avoid pre-filing transfers made with actual intent to prejudice creditors, but the Swiss rule has a five-year lookback and an easier proof rule for related persons, while the U.S. rule uses a two-year lookback and also covers constructive fraud.
Both provisions let a debtor initiate its own bankruptcy case, but the Swiss rule requires the court to confirm insolvency and no realistic debt-settlement prospects before opening the case.

Both provisions govern when creditors’ approval is sufficient to accept a restructuring plan, though Switzerland uses creditor majority/value thresholds while the U.S. rule uses class acceptance mechanics and voting rules.

Both provisions define the bankruptcy estate to include the debtor’s property at the start plus later-acquired property before the case ends, though the U.S. rule also expressly includes post-petition earnings in Chapter 12.
Both provisions govern the final distribution of realized assets to creditors after costs are paid, though the U.S. rule is organized as a bankruptcy priority scheme.

bridges.note: Both provisions allocate a creditor's bankruptcy claim and any surplus between the original creditor and a co-obligor who has paid or may seek reimbursement, but the U.S. rule is more expressly framed as subrogation/reimbursement while the Swiss rule states the claim is still admitted at full amount in the estate.
Both provisions prohibit special ad hoc courts and require a court established by law, but the Swiss text adds broader fair-trial guarantees and venue rules.
Both provisions preserve a creditor’s right to offset mutual pre-bankruptcy claims, while limiting setoff for post-petition or strategically acquired claims.

Both provisions extend a specified set of general bankruptcy rules to a special insolvency proceeding, but the Swiss article is for out-of-court liquidation while the U.S. section is for Chapter 9 municipal bankruptcy.
bridges.b_heading: 11 U.S.C. § 901. Applicability of other sections of this title

bridges.note: Both protect assembly rights, but the German provision is limited to peaceful, unarmed Germans and allows statutory limits for outdoor assemblies, while the Swiss provision broadly guarantees everyone the right to organize, attend, or stay away from assemblies.

Both provisions assign the federal level responsibility for nationwide postal and telecom services, but Germany specifies a mixed public-private regulatory structure while Switzerland directly mandates basic universal service and tariff principles.

Both provisions limit recoverable damages after a fixed time, but the Swiss rule is a general tort prescription period tied to knowledge and absolute deadlines, while the U.S. rule bars patent infringement damages older than six years before suit.

Both provisions regulate the composition of a federal council/upper chamber, but Germany’s Bundesrat represents and is staffed by state governments with weighted votes, while Switzerland’s Bundesrat is a seven-member executive elected by parliament for fixed terms.

Both punish deliberate false or incomplete information given to an authority, but the Swiss rule also covers failure to inform data subjects and refusal to cooperate in investigations, while the U.S. provision is limited to census officials and false sworn statements or returns.

Both provisions require an annual budget to be prepared and submitted to another authority, but the Swiss rule is a formal transmission of the EDÖB’s draft budget through government organs, while the U.S. rule concerns the Postal Service’s detailed business-type budget submitted to OMB under presidential regulations.

Both provisions redistribute public revenues to reduce regional financial disparities, but the German rule is part of revenue allocation within a federal tax system while the Swiss rule expressly sets out a broader intergovernmental equalization scheme with objectives and financing shares.

Both provisions let a public authority set fees for administering a legal process, but the Swiss rule also makes certain documents stamp-free while the U.S. rule specifically concerns design registration services and fee-setting standards.

Both require a yearly report by an oversight/agency head to the legislature, but the Swiss rule also mandates publication and public information in cases of general interest, while the U.S. rule specifies detailed reporting contents to Congress.

Both provisions let a higher authority compel compliance with legal orders, but the German rule authorizes federal coercion against a state while the U.S. rule empowers courts to enforce orders against the Postal Service.

Both provisions give an institutional actor a right to participate and be heard in another body’s proceedings, but the German rule also imposes a duty to attend and keeps the Bundesrat informed, which the U.S. rule does not.

Both protect the home and private life, but Germany’s provision focuses on inviolability and detailed limits on searches and surveillance, while Switzerland’s provision states a broader general privacy right and data protection guarantee.

Both provisions allocate external representation and treaty action to the executive, but Germany gives the Federal President formal treaty powers subject to legislative consent, while Switzerland assigns these tasks to the Federal Council with parliamentary approval.

Both provisions shift liability for wrongful acts of public officials to the public entity, but Article 34 is a general constitutional rule with mandatory recourse and court-access protection, while Article 5 SCHKG is a sector-specific insolvency-law liability rule that also regulates damages, no direct claim against the wrongdoer, and moral compensation.

Both provisions protect property and regulate expropriation, but the German text also guarantees inheritance and sets a detailed constitutional framework for lawful takings and compensation, while the Swiss text is a shorter property guarantee with full compensation for expropriations and equivalent restrictions.
A regulates state supervision, religious instruction, and private schools, while B guarantees a free and sufficient primary education.

Both provisions concern official statistical collection, but the Swiss rule gives the Confederation a general power to gather and harmonize statistics, while the U.S. rule mainly prevents duplicative federal collection and requires access to existing data.

Both provisions regulate a national central bank and monetary authority, but the German rule expressly allows transfer of powers to the EU Central Bank while the Swiss rule keeps the National Bank under federal involvement and adds reserve and profit-allocation rules.
